content: Rubella, also known as German measles, is a contagious disease caused by a virus. Individuals infected with rubella can transmit the virus to others through respiratory droplets when they cough or sneeze. Pregnant women who contract rubella can pass the virus to their developing fetuses. Many individuals infected with rubella may not exhibit any symptoms or may only experience mild symptoms. For those who do develop symptoms, these may include a red rash that begins on the face and spreads to the rest of the body. Additional symptoms can include low-grade fever, headache, mild conjunctivitis (pink eye), general discomfort, swollen and enlarged lymph nodes, cough, and a runny nose. While most adults with rubella experience only mild symptoms, the infection poses significant risks during pregnancy. Pregnant women who contract rubella are at risk of miscarriage or stillbirth, and their developing babies may suffer from severe birth defects with lifelong, devastating consequences. Rubella has been eliminated in regions such as North and South America, including the United States, due to widespread vaccination efforts. However, the disease still exists in other parts of the world. Travelers visiting areas where rubella is present and who are not vaccinated are at risk of infection. Vaccination is the most effective way to protect against rubella. In the United States, the rubella vaccine is routinely administered to children as part of the MMR (measles, mumps, and rubella) or MMRV (measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella) combination vaccines. The vaccine is given in two doses: the first dose is typically administered between 12 and 15 months of age, and the second dose is given between 4 and 6 years of age. Individuals born after 1956 who lack evidence of immunity should receive two doses of the MMR vaccine before traveling, with the second dose administered at least 28 days after the first. People born before 1957 are generally considered immune and do not require vaccination. Infants aged 6 to 11 months who are traveling internationally should receive one dose of the MMR vaccine before travel. However, this dose does not count as part of the routine childhood vaccination series. Pregnant individuals should avoid all exposure to the rubella virus. This includes refraining from receiving the MMR vaccine during pregnancy. Pregnant individuals who are not vaccinated against rubella should avoid traveling to countries or areas with known rubella outbreaks. This precaution is especially critical during the first 20 weeks of pregnancy, as the risk of miscarriage or severe birth defects from rubella infection is highest during this period. Any individual who is pregnant and not already vaccinated against rubella should receive the MMR vaccine immediately after the pregnancy concludes. It is also advised to avoid becoming pregnant for at least four weeks following the administration of the MMR vaccine.
